name: Somray of Battambang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Headley, Robert K., Jr. 1985. Proto-Pearic and the classification of Pearic. In S. Ratanakul, D. Thomas & S. Premsrirat (eds.), Southeast Asian Linguistic Studies Presented to Andre-G. Haudricourt, 428-478. Bangkok: Mahidol University. Open scan:http://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/headley1985proto.pdf(copy consulted).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2 'Phonology', 2.1 'Contemporary phonetic system', pp. 429 (last paragraph) and 431 (first paragraph and the C1/V2/F1 commentary); pp. 2 and 4 of the SEAlang scan. Coverage of Somray: Map 1 p. 430 '1 Somray of Battambang', '10 Samre of Siem Reap'; classification p. 463 '5. NORTH CENTRAL - Somray of Battambang (SY, WP)' and source list p. 469 'Somray of Kranhung, Battambang Prov., Martin' / 'West Pear of Kranhung, Battambang Prov., Baradat' (scan).
catalog_quote: The Pearic word seems to have the same canonic shape as the word in most other Mon-Khmer languages. It consists of a single [p. 431] stressed syllable which may be preceded by a weakly stressed pre-syllable. The formulae below show the various components of the main syllable (MS) and the pre-syllable (PS). ... There are certain limitations on the membership in each one of these components. C1, which represents any consonant that can occur initially at the beginning of a stressed syllable, can be any consonant; ... C3 is any consonant which can occur as the initial consonant in a presyllable, and is apparently limited to /p t k s l/, and C4 is limited to /r/ and /l/. V1 represents any vowel or vowel cluster which can occur as the nucleus of a stressed syllable. Short vowels are not found in open syllables. V2, the vowel nucleus of the presyllable, is a neutral vowel /ə/ which varies between [ɔ-ɑ-a-i]. F1, any final consonant in a stressed syllable, may be /p t c k ʔ m n ñ ŋ v y h r l/ and F2, the final consonant of a presyllable, is limited to /m n ñ ŋ l/. The presyllable is reduced to zero in some of the Chong dialects of Thailand.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Branch-level (Pearic) statement covering Somray of Battambang and Samre of Siem Reap among ten dialects: the word is one stressed main syllable, optionally preceded by a weakly stressed presyllable with a neutral vowel; i.e. stress is on the final (main) syllable of the sesquisyllabic word, predictable from syllable type. No Somray-specific prosodic statement exists in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; presyllable reduced to zero in some Thai Chong dialects (not Somray). Martin 1975 p. 90 notes Somray disyllables often lose their first element ([cənluh] > [nluh]).
new_statements.domain_note: Word (canonic word shape in a comparative phonology); based on wordlists/citation forms (Baradat 1941 ms., Martin 1974a,b, Huffman ms.). Genus-level generalization, not a description of Somray as such.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog somr1240 [smu] bundles Somray of Kranhung, Battambang (Martin's SY, Baradat's West Pear WP; Headley 1985 'North Central' group) with the extinct Somre of Siem Reap (Moura 1883 wordlist only). Martin's 1974b 'Esquisse phonologique du somree' actually describes the Somree of Peam Prus/Anlong Krauch, Pursat Province, which Headley 1985 classifies with 'Samre of Pursat' (his South Central 4.1), i.e. closer to the Samre [sxm] of Ploykaew 2001 (Glottolog samr1245, Trat refugees from the Pursat side) than to Battambang Somray; Glottolog nevertheless files Martin 1974 under somr1240, and Ethnologue places smu in both Pursat and Battambang. The deciding statement quoted here is Headley's Pearic-wide canonic word shape, with Somray of Battambang and Samre of Siem Reap explicitly among the ten dialects it covers; treat as genus-level (pear1246 / west2394), not a Somray-specific description.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Somray language' (accessed 2026-09-17); Glottolog 5.x languoid page somr1240

sources.citation: Pornsawan Ploykaew. 2001. The phonology of Samre. Mon-Khmer Studies 31: 15-27; and 2001 Samre Grammar, PhD thesis, Mahidol University (Samre of Trat, Thailand, ISO sxm = Glottolog samr1245, not this glottocode)
sources.note: Sister lect only (Headley's 'Samre of Pursat' group): MKS 31 p. 17 'The pre-syllables are always unstressed.. The major syllable.. is always stressed'; PhD sec. 2.3 'words are marked by stress and the nuclear syllable may be strongly stressed'. Not usable as first-hand for somr1240.

sources.citation: Martin, Marie Alexandrine. 1975. Les dialectes pear dans leurs rapports avec les langues nationales. Journal of the Siam Society 63(2): 86-95.
sources.note: Fieldworker's own sketch of Somray (Battambang) and Somree (Pursat), visited 1969-72; phonology pp. 88-91 covers consonant mutations, reduction of disyllables to monosyllables in Somray (p. 90: [cənluh] > [nluh] 'torche'), final -r, vowels. No statement on stress or accent placement.

sources.citation: Baradat, R. 1941. Les dialectes des tribus samre. Manuscrit, Ecole Francaise d'Extreme-Orient, Paris. 251 pp. (comparative vocabulary incl. Pear de l'Ouest = West Pear of Kranhung, Battambang)
sources.note: 'Considerations generales': 'Les dialectes samre sont monotoniques'; vowels 'plus appuyees, comme martelees'; 'accent' used only for diacritics. No statement on accent placement; the rest is wordlists.

sources.citation: Baradat, R. 1941. Les Samre ou Pear, population primitive de l'Ouest du Cambodge. BEFEO 41: 1-150.

sources.citation: Diffloth, Gérard. 2012. The four registers of Pearic. Handout presented at the 22nd Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS 22), Agay, France, 2012. 12 pp. (slides, scanned with text). Online athttp://jseals.org/seals22/diffloth2012fourh.pdf(URL given by Sidwell 2023: 78 fn. 6).
sources.note: The handout presents the Pearic lects it cites, Samrai included, as having four registers generated by two features, Clear vs Breathy and Steady vs Constricted ('Glottalized') (chart 'DISTINCTIVE FEATURES of PEARIC REGISTERS', p. 2); comparative tables (pp. 3-6, 8-12) give Samrai forms with register diacritics for c. 45 etyma (dog/tooth/salt, right/left, numerals 1-15, *ʔm-/*ʔn- words, aspiration sets); the 'GLOTTALIZED REGISTERS' slides (pp. 11-12) sort etyma by whether the Pearic glottalized register answers to a segmental *-ʔ- elsewhere in Austroasiatic or only to Chuang /-ʔ-/, with Samrai…
